questions.q: Why does Salesforce enforce governor limits, per this lesson?
options: To generate additional licensing revenue regardless of actual usage
To discourage customers from building any integrations at all
Because governor limits are a legal requirement unrelated to platform architecture
Because Salesforce is a multi-tenant platform, and without hard caps, one org's runaway process could degrade shared infrastructure performance for every other org
questions.explain: Governor limits exist specifically because many different organizations' code and integrations share the same underlying infrastructure — a hard cap prevents one org's runaway process from monopolizing resources that everyone else also depends on.

questions.q: What is the scope of Salesforce's API request limit — is it per integration, or something broader?
options: It is a separate allocation for each individual integration, unaffected by any other integration's usage
It is an org-wide pool shared across every integration, connected app, and user making API calls against that org
It only applies to the Bulk API, never to REST or SOAP calls
It resets every time a new integration is deployed
questions.explain: The daily API request limit is a shared, org-wide pool — every integration, connected app, and user drawing on the same allocation — not a separate allowance carved out per integration, which is why an architect has to consider what else is drawing from that same pool.

questions.q: Why does this lesson instruct the reader to check the org's actual current API allocation rather than memorize a specific number?
options: Because API limits are the same for every org regardless of edition or licensing
Because API limits are irrelevant to integration design
Because the exact daily API allocation depends on the org's edition and licenses, and should be checked in Setup or API response headers rather than assumed
Because Salesforce removed API limits in recent releases
questions.explain: The specific daily API allocation varies by org edition and licensing, so this lesson directs the reader to verify the org's actual current limit (via Setup's System Overview, API usage views, or API response headers) rather than relying on a memorized figure.

questions.q: What is the practical design implication of Salesforce's Apex callout limits (100 per transaction, 120-second cumulative cap) for a high-volume, per-record synchronous integration?
options: It means high-volume, per-record synchronous integration doesn't scale, pointing toward Bulk API or an asynchronous pattern instead
It has no practical implication; synchronous per-record callouts scale to any volume
It means Salesforce cannot make outbound callouts at all
It only applies to SOAP callouts, not REST
questions.explain: The callout caps bound how many synchronous outbound calls a single transaction can realistically make — exactly why high volume per-record synchronous designs hit a wall and Bulk API or asynchronous patterns (Lesson 13) are the correct alternative.

questions.q: What is the difference this lesson draws between a hard-failure limit and a degraded-performance limit?
options: There is no meaningful difference; all limits behave identically
Degraded-performance limits never actually affect production systems
Hard-failure limits only apply to Bulk API, never to Apex

A hard-failure limit (like exceeding the 100-callout cap) throws an exception on that specific transaction immediately, while a degraded-performance limit (like rising concurrent long-running requests) can slow down unrelated transactions gradually without a single pinpointed failure
questions.explain: Some limits (the 100-callout cap) fail a specific transaction outright and immediately once crossed, while others (concurrent long-running requests) degrade shared performance gradually as usage approaches a ceiling, without one transaction's failure pinpointing the exact moment things went wrong.
